principles: Restoration as returning like for like

world_behind.title: Some had misread the doctrine on purpose
world_behind.text: Verse 1 says people have wrested the scriptures and gone far astray on this point. Alma 13:20 has him warn a hostile crowd at Ammonihah in the same words twenty-eight chapters earlier: the scriptures are before you, and wresting them is to your own destruction.

world_behind.title: The chapter continues Alma 40 directly
world_behind.text: Verse 22 of Alma 40 named restoration and verse 24 said this was what the prophets meant. Alma 41 opens on the same word.

world_behind.title: Corianton had a use for the misreading
world_behind.text: Verse 9 tells Corianton not to risk one more offense upon the points of doctrine he has hitherto risked to commit sin. Alma 39:3 names the offense: he forsook the ministry and went after the harlot Isabel. The doctrine is being identified as the cover the conduct used.

world_behind.title: The argument is about the meaning of a word
world_behind.text: Verses 12 and 13 ask what restoration can possibly mean and answer it: bring back again what was sent out. The whole chapter turns on the definition.

world_behind.title: Desires are weighted with works
world_behind.text: Verse 3 counts the desires of the heart alongside the works, and verses 5 and 6 make desire the deciding term twice over.

world_behind.title: The famous line sits in the middle of an argument
world_behind.text: Verse 10 says wickedness never was happiness, and it appears as the conclusion of a proof rather than as a saying on its own.

world_behind.title: The chapter ends on conduct
world_behind.text: Verse 14 turns the doctrine into four instructions: deal justly, judge righteously, do good continually, and have mercy. Alma 7:23 and 24 gives a longer version of the same list to the congregation at Gideon, so the charge to a son ends where a public sermon ended.

words.text: Treated at Alma 8, where the word first appears in this record for twisting a text out of shape. Alma uses it of people who have gone far astray on restoration, and he is about to give the reading he thinks they twisted.

Required, called for by the nature of the case. The word occurs six times in this record and never in the King James Bible. Alma uses it three times in two verses, always with the justice of God, which makes restoration a matter of what justice demands.
Treated at Alma 29:4, where the decrees granted to men according to their desires are unalterable. Here the same unalterable decrees are what leaves the way open to whoever will walk in it.

Belonging to the devil. It appears six times in the record, and the King James Bible once, where James calls a certain wisdom earthly, sensual, and devilish. Alma places it third in a list with evil and carnal, all returning to themselves.

According to what is due. Alma pairs it with mercy, righteous judgment, and continual good in a four-part instruction, and each of the four comes back in the same order in the second half of the verse.
Declares righteous, clears of blame. The record uses it three times and the King James Bible four. Alma's last word on restoration is that it leaves the sinner worse off and offers him no defense.

phrases.term: Some have wrested the scriptures, and have gone far astray because of this thing
phrases.text: Alma names the problem as a misreading before he gives the correction. The doctrine was being used to reach a conclusion it does not support, and he treats that as the reason the explanation is needed.

phrases.term: The plan of restoration is requisite with the justice of God
phrases.text: Restoration is grounded in justice rather than in mercy. Alma repeats requisite three times in two verses, which makes the doctrine a matter of what must follow rather than what might be granted.

phrases.term: If their works were good in this life, and the desires of their hearts were good
phrases.text: Desires are counted alongside works from the first statement. Verses 5 and 6 develop it: a man is raised according to his desires of happiness or of evil, and repentance counts as a desire held to the end.

phrases.term: They are their own judges, whether to do good or do evil
phrases.text: Alma puts the verdict in the hands of the person judged. The sentence sits between being delivered from endless night and the unalterable decrees, and it makes the outcome a matter of what was chosen.

phrases.term: The way is prepared that whosoever will may walk therein and be saved
phrases.text: The decrees are unalterable and the consequence is an open road. Alma uses the fixity of God's law as the reason nobody is shut out rather than as a reason anyone is.

phrases.term: Do not risk one more offense against your God upon those points of doctrine
phrases.text: Alma names what his son did with the misreading. The doctrine had been a licence, and this sentence is the only place in the chapter where the argument becomes personal.
Four words that carry the chapter. Verse 11 gives the reason: a carnal state is contrary to the nature of God and therefore contrary to the nature of happiness, so the two cannot be joined.

phrases.term: Is the meaning of the word restoration to take a thing of a natural state and place it in an unnatural state?
phrases.text: Alma argues from the word itself. He asks what restoring could mean if it produced the opposite of what was there, and lets the question answer itself in the next verse.

phrases.term: Bring back again evil for evil, or carnal for carnal, or devilish for devilish
phrases.text: The definition, given in six matched pairs. Alma runs three negative pairs and then three positive ones, and the symmetry does the arguing.

phrases.term: See that you are merciful unto your brethren; deal justly, judge righteously, and do good continually
phrases.text: Four instructions, and the rest of the verse returns all four in order. Alma turns a doctrine about the last day into a description of this week.

phrases.term: That which ye do send out shall return unto you again, and be restored
phrases.text: The whole chapter compressed. Alma states it as a rule about sending and receiving, then turns the word back on the one it convicts.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: A chapter that exists to correct a misreading
verses.text: The record names its occasion in the first sentence, and the occasion is other people's exegesis: "I have somewhat to say concerning the restoration of which has been spoken; for behold, some have wrested the scriptures, and have gone far astray because of this thing." No misreading is quoted and no reader is named. What follows for fourteen verses is an argument about the meaning of one word, and the word appears in seventeen places across nine of the chapter's fifteen verses.

verses.label: v. 2–4
verses.title: One adjective carrying the structure of the argument
verses.text: Requisite stands in verses 2 and 3 and governs three claims in a row: "the plan of restoration is requisite with the justice of God," "it is requisite that all things should be restored to their proper order," and "it is requisite with the justice of God that men should be judged according to their works." The word is doing legal work, since something requisite is not merely fitting but required by a standard, and the standard is named each time as justice. Verse 4 then draws the conclusion in the same terms: "all things shall be restored to their proper order, every thing to its natural frame."

verses.label: v. 10
verses.title: A prohibition on an inference, and a flat sentence
verses.text: The correction is stated as a rule about what may not be concluded: "Do not suppose, because it has been spoken concerning restoration, that ye shall be restored from sin to happiness." What follows is the shortest sentence in the chapter and it makes no reference to restoration at all: "wickedness never was happiness." Four words state a claim about the past tense of a category, and the record offers no argument for it here or anywhere else.

verses.label: v. 11
verses.title: A phrase revised mid-clause and both versions kept
verses.text: The record preserves the correction rather than the corrected text: "all men that are in a state of nature, or I would say, in a carnal state, are in the gall of bitterness and in the bonds of iniquity." The same speaker does this at Alma 40:2, "there is no resurrection, or, I would say, in other words," and Amulek does it at Alma 10:5, "but behold, I mistake." Three times the volume prints a first attempt, the marker, and the replacement.

verses.label: v. 12–13
verses.title: A definition reached by rejecting a wrong one
verses.text: The record puts the false reading as a question, "is the meaning of the word restoration to take a thing of a natural state and place it in an unnatural state, or to place it in a state opposite to its nature?", and answers it in four words: "O, my son, this is not the case." Only then does the definition arrive, and it comes as seven matched pairs: "evil for evil, or carnal for carnal, or devilish for devilish, good for that which is good; righteous for that which is righteous; just for that which is just; merciful for that which is merciful." The form of the sentence is the argument, since each pair returns the same term to itself.

verses.label: v. 14
verses.title: Four commands, in a chapter that has had none
verses.text: After thirteen verses of definition the register changes without warning: "see that you are merciful unto your brethren; deal justly, judge righteously, and do good continually." Merciful, just, righteous and good are the same four terms verse 13 has just used as the right-hand side of its pairs. The imperatives are therefore not a change of subject but the doctrine turned into instructions, and the record makes the connection only in the verse that follows.

chapter.title: The chapter is a dispute over a definition
chapter.text: The word "restore" and its forms run through the chapter and verse 13 supplies the definition by listing pairs, "evil for evil, or carnal for carnal, or devilish for devilish—good for that which is good; righteous for that which is righteous; just for that which is just." Verse 10 rules out the reading being corrected in six words, "wickedness never was happiness." Verse 15 states the consequence for the argument, "the word restoration more fully condemneth the sinner, and justifieth him not at all." A doctrinal dispute is settled by defining one term and running it symmetrically in both directions.

chapter.title: Restoration is grounded in justice
chapter.text: Requisite turns up three times across two verses, tied each time to what justice requires. Alma does not argue that God chooses to return like for like; he argues that justice requires it.

chapter.title: Desire is counted, and not only action
chapter.text: Verse 3 pairs works with the desires of the heart, and verses 5 and 6 make desire the operative term. A man is raised according to what he wanted.

chapter.title: The famous line is a conclusion
chapter.text: Wickedness never was happiness arrives after the argument about natures and before the explanation in verse 11. It is the middle of a proof.

chapter.title: He names how his son used the doctrine
chapter.text: Verse 9 says Corianton risked offenses upon these points. The chapter is not abstract; it removes a specific excuse.

chapter.title: The unalterable decrees are good news here
chapter.text: Alma 29 used the same word for something he could not argue with. Here the fixity of the law is the reason the road stays open to anyone who will walk it.

chapter.title: The symmetry of verse 13 is the proof
chapter.text: Three negative pairs and three positive ones, in matched form. The structure of the sentence is doing the persuading.

chapter.title: Doctrine ends as instruction
chapter.text: Verse 14 gives four things to do and returns all four as things received. Alma closes a chapter about the last day with what to do about tomorrow.

applications.title: Watch your desires, not only your conduct
applications.text: Alma puts what a man wanted beside what he did, twice over, and makes both of them terms of the restoration. Ask what you have wanted this week that you would not have done, and put it on the same page as what you did.

applications.title: Check whether a belief is licensing you
applications.text: Corianton had used a doctrine to make room for something. Take the belief you find most comfortable and ask what it currently permits you that you would otherwise question.

applications.title: Refuse the reading that would suit you
applications.text: The correction is six words long: "wickedness never was happiness." Alma does not argue the point, he blocks it. When a chain of reasoning arrives somewhere you know is false, the fastest repair is to say so and go back for the faulty link.

applications.title: Name the state you are reasoning from
applications.text: Alma describes the natural condition plainly, "in the gall of bitterness and in the bonds of iniquity," before he explains what restoration does. Any account of where you are going needs an honest account of where it starts.

applications.title: Ask what the word actually means
applications.text: Alma settled the question by defining one term and running it in both directions. When an argument turns on a word, write down what you take it to mean before continuing.

applications.title: Do the four things in order
applications.text: Be merciful, deal justly, judge righteously, do good continually. The list is short, ordinary, and entirely about other people. Take the one you are worst at and give it a week.

applications.title: Send out what you want back
applications.text: Mercy, justice, righteous judgment. The rule is stated as a mechanism rather than a reward, "that which ye do send out shall return unto you again." Decide what you would want restored, and then look at what you are actually sending.

questions.text: What scripture have I read in a way that suited me?
If my desires were judged today, what would they show?
In what sense am I already my own judge?
What doctrine have I leaned on to keep doing something?
Where am I still expecting wickedness to make me happy?
What am I sending out, honestly?
Which of the four does my life show least of?
